summary: Audi's new-generation Q5 e-hybrid quattro is the plug-in the brand badged TFSI e last time round, and its headline is price parity: at $96,900 for the SUV and $100,400 for the Sportback it costs exactly the same as the 200kW TFSI quattro sport petrol while making 270kW/500Nm and adding 82km of WLTP electric range from a 20.7kWh usable battery. That undercuts the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e and the BMW X3 30e while carrying more claimed electric range than the BMW, and reviewers rate the PPC-platform Q5's new-found ride comfort and cabin technology highly. The reservations are consistent and not about the powertrain: capacitive touch panels have replaced most physical controls, the steering is over-assisted, the battery costs 82 litres of boot, and with the PHEV FBT exemption gone since April 2025 the case rests entirely on charging at home.
pros: 270kW/500Nm and 5.1sec to 100km/h for exactly the same $96,900 (SUV) / $100,400 (Sportback) as the 200kW TFSI quattro sport petrol — 70kW more for no extra money, and it undercuts the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e ($99,900) and BMW X3 30e ($104,800)
82km WLTP electric range from a 20.7kWh usable (25.9kWh gross) battery, about 45 per cent more capacity than the old Q5 55 TFSI e, so a typical 30-45km Melbourne commute runs on electricity alone
11kW three-phase AC charging fills the pack 0-100 per cent in about 2.5 hours, up from 7.2kW on the superseded Q5 TFSI e, which makes daytime top-ups practical rather than overnight-only

75g/km combined CO2 is well under Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car threshold, so it pays $8.40 per $200 duty instead of the $10.40 (SUV) or $14.00 (Sportback) per $200 an equivalently priced petrol Q5 attracts — worth roughly $970 on the SUV and $2,800 on the Sportback

2000kg braked towing plus standard 20-inch Audi Sport wheels, sport suspension, red calipers, black styling pack, privacy glass and auxiliary air-conditioning that the same-priced petrol does not get; five-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with the high-voltage battery covered eight years/160,000km
cons: The battery under the boot floor costs 82 litres: 438L seats-up in the SUV and 433L in the Sportback, against 520L in the petrol and diesel Q5, and 1358L/1300L folded versus 1473L — the Mercedes GLC 350e carries 590L and the BMW X3 30e 460L

The 3.3L/100km ADR label figure only holds if you start every trip charged: Audi's own WLTP figure with the battery discharged is 7.4-8.4L/100km for the 270kW car and an independent charge-sustaining test returned 7.8L/100km, so an apartment-dwelling buyer is running a 2170kg petrol SUV on 95 RON

AC-only charging capped at 11kW with no DC fast-charge hardware at all, where the Mercedes GLC 350e accepts up to 60kW DC — a flat battery on a road trip stays flat until you find a destination charger

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and both variants sit above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and far above the $75,000 FBT phase cap, so the novated-lease concessions that once justified the plug-in premium no longer apply

Reviewers are consistent that the new Q5 trades away driver engagement and usability: steering with too much electronic assist, climate and most secondary functions moved to capacitive touch panels, a tight rear seat with a high floor hump, and a tyre repair kit rather than a spare
